title: Ultrasound Lets Scientists Check 'Pregnant' Coral Without Harming It
summary:
Coral can now get a checkup without being cut open. Scientists have used an ultrasound machine to look inside living coral underwater and spot eggs developing within it. It is the first time researchers can assess a coral's reproductive health without harming or sacrificing the animal.

Until now, checking whether coral was carrying eggs usually meant cutting it open. The new approach uses sound waves instead. Canon, the camera maker, announced this week that its advanced medical ultrasound platform, the Aplio i700, can scan coral submerged underwater. With the United Kingdom conservation group Coral Spawning International, the team scanned six species of large polyp stony coral. Its high and ultra-high frequency probes let researchers see through the corals' skeletons.

To confirm the scans, the team cut open one coral species, Trachyphyllia geoffroyi, and took high-powered images of its interior. The images matched the ultrasound results, confirming that the structures seen in the scans were indeed eggs.

Knowing when corals will release their eggs matters. It can help conservationists predict spawning and time their restoration work, giving breeding programs a head start. Ultrasound scans could make that work more precise while sparing corals from being cut apart.

Coral needs all the help it can get. Late last month, the International Union for Conservation of Nature warned that nearly all of Earth's coral reef ecosystems, 96 percent, face an extremely high risk of collapse within the next 50 years, driven by warming oceans and heat waves. Reefs, sometimes called the rainforests of the sea, support an estimated quarter of all marine species. When reefs collapse, coral dies and is replaced by algae and sponges that support far less marine life.
why_it_matters: Reefs support about a quarter of all marine species, and nearly all reef ecosystems face an extremely high risk of collapse, so a gentle way to track coral reproduction can help conservationists protect and rebuild them.

background_read: Coral is a living animal that builds a hard skeleton, and many corals release eggs into the water so new corals can grow.
An ultrasound machine sends sound waves into the body and builds a picture from the echoes, which lets doctors look inside a person without surgery.
Scientists are now using that same idea underwater to see eggs growing inside living coral, so they can tell when the coral is ready to spawn.
Knowing when spawning will happen helps conservationists plan their work to protect and restore reefs, which support many kinds of ocean life.
